title: Colchicine and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Gout, Gut and Toxicity Risks
excerpt: Can you drink on colchicine? How alcohol worsens colchicine's gut side effects, triggers gout flares, and strains the organs that clear the drug, plus the warning signs that need a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink alcohol on colchicine? How it worsens gut side effects, triggers gout flares, and affects toxicity risk, plus warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for many people on a steady, low dose of colchicine, an occasional drink is not dangerous, and plenty of doctors allow it. But "colchicine and alcohol" is a worse pairing than it looks for two reasons. First, both hit your gut: colchicine's most common side effects are diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting, and alcohol irritates the same system. Second, and more important, alcohol (especially beer and spirits) raises uric acid and is a well-known trigger for gout attacks, so drinking can undo the very thing colchicine is helping with. There's also a quieter risk: anything that strains your liver or kidneys, or dries you out, can let colchicine build up, and colchicine has a narrow safety margin.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink during a gout flare, especially on days you're taking flare-sized doses. On a low daily dose, keep any drinking light, choose wine over beer if you drink at all, and match every drink with water. Never take extra colchicine because you drank or because a flare started after drinking, beyond what your doctor's flare plan says. If you get severe diarrhea or vomiting, muscle weakness, numbness, or unusual bruising, stop and call your doctor.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and prescribing guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history, dose, and other medicines. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking** if you take colchicine and you also have kidney or liver disease, take a statin, certain antibiotics, antifungals, HIV medicines, heart medicines, or other drugs your pharmacist has flagged, or if you drink most days. **Get urgent care or call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) if** you may have taken more colchicine than prescribed, or you have severe or nonstop diarrhea or vomiting, muscle weakness, numbness or tingling, unusual bleeding or bruising, fever or sore throat, or you're passing very little urine. In an emergency, call 911.

## What Colchicine Does and Why It Needs Respect

Colchicine is an old drug, first purified from the autumn crocus plant, and it's still a front-line medicine today. Doctors prescribe it for:

- **Gout flares**, to calm the joint inflammation once an attack starts.
- **Gout prevention**, usually as a low daily dose for the first several months after starting a urate-lowering drug like allopurinol, when flares are more likely.
- **Familial Mediterranean fever**, an inherited inflammatory condition.
- **Pericarditis**, inflammation of the sac around the heart.
- **Heart disease risk reduction**, where a low-dose version (sold in the US as Lodoco) was approved in 2023 for some adults with heart disease.

It works in an unusual way. Colchicine sticks to a protein called tubulin, which cells use to build tiny internal scaffolding (microtubules). White blood cells called neutrophils need that scaffolding to rush into an inflamed joint and keep the inflammation going. With colchicine on board, they can't mobilize as well, so the inflammation settles. Colchicine also dampens an inflammation "alarm" inside immune cells known as the inflammasome, which is triggered by uric acid crystals.

The catch is that colchicine affects *all* fast-dividing cells a little, not just the ones in your joint. That's why the cells lining your gut, which renew constantly, are the first to complain: diarrhea, cramping, nausea, and vomiting are its most common side effects. It's also why colchicine has a **narrow therapeutic index**, which means the gap between a helpful dose and a harmful one is small. At the doses doctors prescribe, it's safe for most people. When it builds up, it can damage muscles, nerves, and bone marrow, and serious overdoses can be fatal.

That narrow margin is the lens to look at alcohol through. The question isn't really "does alcohol poison colchicine?" It's "does alcohol do anything that pushes colchicine levels up, or piles more stress on the systems colchicine already stresses?"

## How Colchicine and Alcohol Actually Interact

There are four real ways the two overlap. None of them is the dramatic "never mix these" reaction you'd get with something like metronidazole, but together they explain why doctors usually say "go easy."

### 1. They pile onto the same gut side effects

This is the one most people notice. Colchicine's gut effects are common enough that the classic way of dosing it for flares used to be "keep taking it until the pain stops or diarrhea starts." Modern dosing is much gentler for exactly that reason (more on that below).

Alcohol irritates the stomach lining, speeds up how fast things move through the intestines, and interferes with how the gut absorbs water. That's why so many people get loose stools after a night out. (Our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) explains why in more detail.)

Put the two together and you have two causes of the same problem stacked on top of each other. A mild case is just unpleasant. A bad case can leave you dehydrated, and dehydration matters more than usual when you're on colchicine, which brings us to the next point.

### 2. Dehydration and kidney strain can let colchicine build up

Your kidneys handle a meaningful share of colchicine clearance, and the prescribing information calls for lower doses or extra caution in people with reduced kidney function. Alcohol is a diuretic: it suppresses the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you lose more fluid than you take in. Add vomiting or diarrhea and you can become properly dry.

In a healthy person with normal kidneys, a night of moderate drinking isn't likely to push colchicine into a dangerous range. But if your kidneys are already borderline (which is common in people with long-standing gout), or you're losing fluid from both ends, the safety margin shrinks. This is one reason colchicine side effects can show up after an illness with vomiting and diarrhea even when the dose hasn't changed.

### 3. Liver stress affects how colchicine is cleared

Colchicine is broken down in the liver by an enzyme called **CYP3A4**, and it's pumped out of cells by a transporter called **P-glycoprotein (P-gp)**. This is where colchicine's best-known interaction warnings come from. Drugs that strongly block CYP3A4 or P-gp, such as clarithromycin, certain antifungals like ketoconazole, some HIV medicines, cyclosporine, and some heart drugs, can raise colchicine levels sharply. Grapefruit juice is on the caution list for the same reason. The US prescribing information has detailed dose-reduction tables for these combinations.

Alcohol itself isn't a recognized strong CYP3A4 or P-gp blocker, and it's not on those lists. A drink doesn't "lock" colchicine in your body the way clarithromycin can. The concern with alcohol is longer-term: heavy, regular drinking damages the liver, and colchicine needs extra caution in people with liver disease. For a social drinker with a healthy liver, this point is mostly a reason not to let occasional drinking become daily heavy drinking.

### 4. Both can affect muscles and blood cells

Colchicine's rare but serious side effects include muscle damage (myopathy, sometimes with nerve involvement) and a drop in blood cells from the bone marrow. Heavy long-term drinking can cause its own muscle problems and can also suppress the bone marrow. The risk of colchicine muscle problems is higher in people who also take a statin, which many people with gout do because gout and heart disease often travel together. If that's you, our guides to [statins and alcohol](/never-hungover/statins-and-alcohol) and [atorvastatin and alcohol](/never-hungover/atorvastatin-and-alcohol) cover that side of the picture.

None of this means one drink will damage your muscles. It means that muscle pain or weakness while you're on colchicine deserves a call to your doctor rather than being written off as a hangover. (Normal post-drinking aches are covered in our guide to [body aches after drinking](/never-hungover/body-aches-after-drinking).)

## The Bigger Problem: Alcohol Triggers the Gout Colchicine Is Treating

For most people searching this topic, the reason they're on colchicine is gout. And here, the research on alcohol is much clearer than the research on any direct drug interaction.

### Why alcohol raises uric acid

Gout happens when uric acid builds up in the blood and forms sharp crystals in a joint. Alcohol raises uric acid in a few ways at once:

- **It slows uric acid removal.** When your liver processes alcohol, it produces lactate. Your kidneys use the same exit route for lactate and uric acid, so more lactate means less uric acid gets flushed out.
- **It speeds up uric acid production.** Breaking down alcohol uses up the cell's energy molecules quickly, and the leftover pieces are converted into uric acid.
- **Some drinks add purines directly.** Purines are compounds that the body turns into uric acid. Beer is relatively high in them, which is one reason it stands out in the research.
- **It dehydrates you.** Less fluid means more concentrated uric acid, which makes crystals more likely to form.

### What the studies show

The best-known study here followed about 47,000 male health professionals for 12 years and was published in *The Lancet* in 2004 by Hyon Choi and colleagues. The risk of developing gout rose with total alcohol intake. Beer had the strongest link, spirits a weaker one, and moderate wine drinking was not clearly linked to higher risk in that study.

A later study by Yuqing Zhang and colleagues (published in *The American Journal of Medicine* in 2014) looked at people who already had gout and asked what they'd had to drink in the day or two before each flare. Drinking more alcohol in that short window was linked with a higher chance of a flare, and this held for wine as well as beer and spirits. That matters for anyone who thinks switching to wine gives them a free pass.

The 2020 American College of Rheumatology gout guideline reflects this, recommending that people with gout limit alcohol intake regardless of how active their disease is.

### What this means if you're on colchicine

If you take daily colchicine to prevent flares while your urate-lowering medicine kicks in, drinking can produce flares that "break through" the colchicine. It's easy to conclude the medicine isn't working when the drinking is the bigger driver. If you take colchicine only when a flare starts, drinking makes it more likely you'll need it, and more often, which means more courses of a drug whose side effects mostly land on your gut.

In other words, the most important reason to be careful with alcohol on colchicine isn't a chemical clash. It's that the alcohol and the medicine are pulling in opposite directions.

## Can You Drink Alcohol While Taking Colchicine?

There's no blanket answer, and the honest version depends on which kind of colchicine user you are.

**If you're on a low daily preventive dose and your gout is under control:** many doctors are comfortable with light, occasional drinking. "Light" means a drink or two, not a big night. Pick wine over beer or spirits, drink water alongside it, eat beforehand, and notice whether drinking is followed by flares or stomach trouble. If it is, that's useful information to bring to your doctor.

**If you're in the middle of a flare:** skip it. This is when uric acid is already causing trouble, when the higher flare doses of colchicine are most likely to upset your stomach, and when dehydration would do the most harm.

**If you take colchicine for pericarditis, familial Mediterranean fever, or heart protection:** the gout-trigger issue matters less, but the gut side effects, dehydration, and liver and kidney considerations still apply. Ask your prescriber what they're comfortable with.

**If you have kidney or liver disease, take a statin, or take any drug your pharmacist has flagged as interacting with colchicine:** talk to your doctor before drinking at all. These are the situations where colchicine is most likely to build up, and where adding alcohol's effects leaves the least room for error.

## Colchicine and Beer: Why Beer Gets Singled Out

Beer comes up so often with gout that it deserves its own section. It combines alcohol's effects on uric acid with a meaningful load of purines from brewing yeast and grains. That double hit is why beer has had the strongest link with gout in large studies.

Two practical notes:

- **Non-alcoholic beer isn't automatically gout-safe.** Removing the alcohol removes one part of the problem, but beer's purines come from the grain and yeast, not the alcohol. There's limited research on non-alcoholic beer and gout specifically, so treat it as "better than regular beer," not "free." If you're curious what's actually in it, see our guide on [whether non-alcoholic beer has alcohol](/never-hungover/does-non-alcoholic-beer-have-alcohol).
- **A few beers at a game is a classic flare setup.** A big volume of beer, salty food, and not much water, often followed by sleeping in a dehydrated state, is a common story behind morning-after gout attacks.

If you're on colchicine and beer is your drink, that's the single change most likely to cut down your flares.

## Colchicine, Alcohol, and Flare Days: Doses Matter

How colchicine is dosed during a flare explains why flare days are the worst time to drink.

For a gout flare, the US label for colchicine 0.6 mg tablets (Colcrys) directs **1.2 mg at the first sign of a flare, then 0.6 mg one hour later**, for a maximum of 1.8 mg over that hour. This "low-dose" approach came from a randomized trial (the AGREE trial, published in 2010) which found it worked about as well as the old high-dose approach for early flares, with far fewer stomach side effects. Your doctor may give you a different plan, especially if you're already on a daily preventive dose or take interacting medicines, so follow theirs.

Two things stand out:

1. **The flare dose is when gut side effects peak.** Adding alcohol right then stacks two sources of diarrhea and nausea.
2. **More is not better.** If a flare doesn't settle, the answer is not to take extra colchicine, and certainly not to take extra after drinking. Taking more than prescribed is the most common route to colchicine toxicity. Call your doctor instead. They may add or switch to a different flare treatment.

## How Long After Colchicine Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period, and timing tricks don't help much. Colchicine leaves the body slowly: its elimination half-life in healthy adults is roughly a day or more, according to the prescribing information. If you take it daily, it's always on board. Waiting four hours after a dose doesn't meaningfully clear it.

So instead of watching the clock, the useful questions are:

- **Am I in a flare?** If yes, don't drink.
- **Have my kidneys or liver been flagged as a concern?** If yes, ask your doctor before drinking at all.
- **Am I on any other medicines that interact with colchicine?** If yes, check with your pharmacist.
- **How much am I planning to drink?** One drink is a very different question from five.

If the answers are "no flare, healthy organs, no flagged medicines, one or two drinks," most people are in the zone where an occasional drink is low risk. Eat first, alternate with water, and stop if your stomach starts protesting.

## Can You Take Colchicine for a Hangover?

No, and it's worth saying plainly because people sometimes reach for whatever is in the cabinet. Colchicine is not a painkiller or a general anti-inflammatory. It does nothing for hangover headache, nausea, or fatigue, and it would add stomach upset and diarrhea to a body that's already dehydrated. Only take it as prescribed.

If a night of drinking leaves you with a hot, swollen, very painful joint (often the big toe, but also the ankle, knee, or wrist), that's likely a gout flare, not a hangover. Follow the flare plan your doctor gave you, rest the joint, drink water, and call your doctor if it isn't improving or you have a fever.

What about other painkillers? Doctors often use NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen for gout flares, sometimes alongside colchicine. Those carry their own alcohol warning about stomach bleeding, which you can read about in our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol). Steroids like prednisone are another flare option with their own alcohol considerations, covered in [prednisone and alcohol](/never-hungover/prednisone-and-alcohol). Aspirin, even at low doses, can affect uric acid levels and isn't usually the go-to for gout pain.

## Warning Signs: When to See a Doctor

Most people on colchicine never have a serious problem. But because the drug has a narrow safety margin, these signs need attention rather than "sleeping it off."

> **Call your doctor promptly if you notice:**
> - Diarrhea, nausea, or vomiting that is severe, lasts more than a day, or keeps you from keeping fluids down
> - Muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, especially in the thighs or shoulders, or trouble climbing stairs
> - Numbness, tingling, or burning in your hands or feet
> - Unusual bruising or bleeding, or very pale skin, lips, or nails
> - Fever, chills, sore throat, or other signs of infection
> - A gout flare that isn't improving after following your plan
>
> **Get emergency help (911 in the US) or call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) right away if:**
> - You or someone else may have taken more colchicine than prescribed, even if they feel fine right now
> - There is severe vomiting or diarrhea with dizziness, fainting, confusion, or very little urine
> - Breathing is difficult, or someone is very weak or hard to wake

A note on overdose: colchicine poisoning often starts with gut symptoms that look like a stomach bug or a bad hangover, and the serious damage to blood cells and organs can follow a day or more later. That delay is why you should call Poison Control early if too much was taken, rather than waiting to see how things go. Keep colchicine out of reach of children; small amounts can be dangerous for them.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You have less room for error with colchicine and alcohol if you:

- **Have kidney disease or reduced kidney function.** Colchicine clearance drops, and alcohol's dehydrating effect adds to the strain.
- **Have liver disease** or have been told your liver enzymes are high.
- **Take a statin** (such as atorvastatin or simvastatin) or a fibrate, because the risk of colchicine-related muscle problems goes up.
- **Take a drug that blocks CYP3A4 or P-gp**, such as clarithromycin, erythromycin, ketoconazole or itraconazole, certain HIV medicines, cyclosporine, verapamil, or diltiazem. Your pharmacist can check your list.
- **Are older**, since kidney function naturally declines with age and side effects are more likely.
- **Drink most days or drink heavily** when you do drink.

If several of these apply, the safest plan is to discuss alcohol with your doctor directly rather than relying on general advice. For a broader look at how common medicines and supplements interact with alcohol, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Practical Tips If You Choose to Drink

If your doctor has said an occasional drink is fine, these habits keep the risk low:

1. **Never drink during a flare** or on days you're taking flare doses.
2. **Keep it light.** One or two drinks, not a session.
3. **Choose wine over beer and spirits** if you drink, and remember that less of anything is better than more of the "right" drink.
4. **Drink water alongside every drink**, and before bed. Staying hydrated helps your kidneys clear both uric acid and colchicine.
5. **Eat first.** Food slows alcohol absorption and makes stomach upset less likely.
6. **Don't change your colchicine dose** because you drank. Don't skip it to "make room," and don't add extra.
7. **Watch the pattern.** If flares or stomach trouble keep following drinks, that's a sign to cut back further and talk to your doctor about your gout plan.
8. **Don't add grapefruit juice** to your mixers, since it's on colchicine's caution list.

Long-term, the biggest win for most people with gout is getting uric acid under control with a urate-lowering medicine. Once uric acid stays at target for a while, flares become much less frequent, and the daily preventive colchicine is often stopped. That's usually a better path to enjoying the occasional drink than trying to out-medicate a drinking habit.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Since this is a site about drinking smarter, it's worth being clear about supplements here.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human research. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents gout, lowers uric acid in people, or reduces colchicine side effects, and it doesn't change any of the advice above.

There's also an interaction question worth flagging. Colchicine is unusually sensitive to anything that affects CYP3A4 and P-gp, and lab studies suggest that some plant flavonoids, a family that includes DHM, can influence drug-processing enzymes. Whether DHM does this to a meaningful degree in people is unknown. Because colchicine's safety margin is narrow, **ask your pharmacist before adding DHM or any other supplement while you take colchicine.**

If you get the go-ahead and you're looking for a DHM product for the occasional night out, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the strongest evidence, which matter more than any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Colchicine and alcohol don't have a dramatic chemical clash, and for many people on a stable low dose, an occasional light drink is acceptable. The real risks are practical: both upset your gut, alcohol dehydrates you and can strain the kidneys and liver that clear colchicine, and alcohol (beer most of all) raises uric acid and triggers the gout flares colchicine is meant to control. Skip alcohol during flares, keep any drinking light and well-hydrated, never adjust your colchicine dose because you drank, and treat severe diarrhea, muscle weakness, numbness, or unusual bruising as reasons to call your doctor. If you have kidney or liver disease or take interacting medicines, get personal advice before you drink.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking colchicine?**

Many doctors are fine with an occasional drink for people on colchicine, but there is no single rule, and the answer depends on why you take it, your dose, your kidneys and liver, and your other medicines. Alcohol doesn't block colchicine the way some antibiotics or grapefruit juice do. The main problems are that both cause stomach upset and diarrhea, and alcohol (especially beer and spirits) can trigger the gout flares colchicine is meant to treat. Ask your doctor or pharmacist what's reasonable for you.

**Is it safe to drink alcohol during a gout flare while taking colchicine?**

It's best not to. Alcohol raises uric acid and can make a flare worse or last longer, and the higher flare-day doses of colchicine are when stomach side effects are most likely. Drinking at the same time stacks nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea on top of each other and makes dehydration more likely. Skip alcohol until the flare has settled and you're back on your usual routine.

**Does alcohol make colchicine less effective?**

There's no good evidence that alcohol changes how colchicine is absorbed or broken down in a meaningful way. The bigger issue is practical: alcohol raises uric acid and is a well-documented trigger for gout attacks, so drinking can work against the reason you're taking colchicine in the first place. You may feel like the medicine 'isn't working' when the drinking is driving new flares.

**How long after taking colchicine can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period. Colchicine stays in the body for a long time (its half-life is roughly a day or more), so waiting a few hours doesn't clear it. People taking a low daily preventive dose usually can't time around it anyway. A more useful approach is to avoid alcohol on flare days, keep any drinking light on other days, drink water alongside it, and ask your doctor what limit makes sense for you.

**Is beer worse than wine for gout if I take colchicine?**

In large studies, beer has had the strongest link with gout and higher uric acid, spirits a weaker link, and moderate wine the weakest. That doesn't make wine safe: a study of people who already had gout found that drinking any type of alcohol in the previous day or two was linked with a higher chance of a flare. If you drink, small amounts of wine are generally considered a lower-risk choice than beer, but less overall is what matters most.

**What are the warning signs of colchicine toxicity?**

Early signs are severe or persistent diarrhea, vomiting, and stomach pain. Later signs include muscle weakness or pain, numbness or tingling in the hands or feet, unusual bleeding or bruising, fever, sore throat or other signs of infection, feeling very weak or faint, and passing very little urine. Colchicine overdose can be life-threatening. If you think you or someone else took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US) or 911 right away.

**Can I take colchicine for a hangover or after a night of drinking?**

No. Colchicine is a prescription anti-inflammatory for specific conditions like gout and pericarditis. It does nothing for hangovers and would add stomach upset and diarrhea to a body that's already dehydrated. Only take it as your doctor prescribed. If a night of drinking set off a gout flare, follow the flare plan your doctor gave you.

**Is it safe to take DHM with colchicine?**

There's no human research on combining DHM with colchicine. Colchicine is sensitive to anything that affects the liver enzyme and transporter that clear it, and lab studies suggest some plant flavonoids can influence drug-processing enzymes, though how much that matters in people is unclear. Because colchicine has a narrow safety margin, ask your pharmacist before adding DHM or any other supplement. DHM does not treat or prevent gout.
